newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Ex-general says Algeria politics "permanent coups".
newsitem.headline: Ex-general says Algeria politics "permanent coups".

text.p: Algeria's first fighter pilot, later a senior general who retired five months ago, described Algeria's political system as a permanent coup d'etat over 33 years.

"All these successive regimes established against the people's will were coups d'etat. In fact they were a one permanent coup," said general Yahia Rahal, who qualified as the first Algerian to fly a fighter aircraft and who later held several senior positions in the military.

Rahal makes his assessment of the Algerian political scene in a newly written book entitled "Coups d'etat", which he said in an interview with El Watan newspaper on Monday gives an insider's insight into Algeria's political evolution.

Algeria, run for nearly three decades as a one-party state, last week elected its first plural National Assembly (lower house). Supporters of President Liamine Zeroual, also a former general, emerged as the leading political force with 155 seats in the 380-member lower house.
With the book's publication, Rahal becomes the first senior army officer to break the silence tightly kept by the army round its generals over politics. Algerians bill their army "the great mute".
He said he had preferred that the book go for sale after last Thursday's general election to avoid influencing the poll.

The former general said Algeria has been ruled by a succession of coup d'etat leaders, starting with those of a provisional government who kept Houari Boumedienne from power on the eve of the country's independence from France in 1962.
Boumedienne kept a tight grip on the army until he succeeded in arranging the election of president Ahmed Ben Bella, whom he in turn overthrew in 1965.
A conclave of military leaders ensured that their man Chadli Benjedid took over when Boumedienne died in 1978.
And army generals were said to have forced Chadli to step down in 1992 to prevent Moslem militants from taking power after they took a huge lead in a free parliamentary election they scrapped.
A military-dominated council then appointed a five-man presidential body to rule the country until the appointement of President Liamine Zeroual by the same council in 1994.
Zeroual, however, was returned to power in Algeria's first plural presidential election in November 1995.

"I consider that testifying in writing on events does not mean fuelling the fire (of the country's crisis) but is on the contrary aimed to help finding means to bring the fire under control," Rahal told El Watan newspaper.
He urged other senior officials to follow his example in shedding lights on main events to help fill a shortage of information in the past three decades.
"...Any information is welcome, especially in our country where we have been weaned from true information during more than 35 years," he said.
